## Abstract

How should we go about collecting evidence when we’re looking to settle some

question? In this thesis, I develop and defend an account of the evaluative and

normative epistemic dimensions intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering.

Chapter 1 introduces the topic. Chapter 2 is devoted to laying out the positive

proposal, which makes use of the notions of accuracy and competence to spell

out the conditions under which an act of evidence-gathering is successful,

rational, and skillful. It also shows how the account can be applied to the

simple case of inquiry into polar questions as well as to the more complex

cases of inquiry into wh-questions and subject matters. Chapters 3 and 4

provide arguments for accepting the account. Chapter 3 zooms in on the

central notion of the proposed account, accuracy gain, and argues that such a

notion independently provides the best available measure of information value,

namely the usefulness of a certain piece of information given the aim of settling

a certain question. This is done by showing that accuracy gain fares better than

competing measures from information theory, Bayesian statistics, and decision

theory on a number of fronts. Chapter 4 ﬁrst looks at how the proposed account

fares vis-à-vis three main competing views about the aim of inquiry, arguing

that it emerges as superior in several respects. Then, the Chapter considers

three objections that may be raised against the proposed account, and argues

## Chapter 1

## Introduction

This thesis begins with three simple stories:

The Detective. At a summer mansion by the coast, there’s been a

murder. The detective has been called on the phone, and is already

on her way to the crime scene. On the car, she thinks about how

she should proceed. She needs evidence in order to ﬁnd out who

committed the crime. What she is thinking about right now is how

best to collect such evidence. She knows that under interrogation,

sometimes ﬂaws can be found in the professed alibis of guilty indi-

viduals. But for that, one needs to ask the right questions. She also

knows that ﬁnding the murder weapon would be a breakthrough in

the investigation. But for that, one needs to look in the right places.

The Lab. A group of scientists has just received a major grant, which

allows them to pursue their research project. What they now need

to do is gather as much data as possible. The data is collected via

experiments, and the experiments need special equipment. Unfor-

tunately, the grant can only cover the purchase of a limited amount

of such equipment. So, they sit down and discuss what experiments

it would be best to pursue.

The Curious Layperson. José just watched a documentary which

sparked in him an interest in the issue of whether human beings

have free will. He decides to read a book to gain more information

on the matter. He knows that this is a controversial topic on which

people have held a variety of views, and that reading diﬀerent books

will plausibly lead him to formulate diﬀerent thoughts on the topic.

After looking at the front cover of a number of books, he is now

thinking carefully about which one to buy.

These three cases share an important feature. The detective, the group of

scientists, and the curious layperson all need to collect evidence so that they

can get closer to, and possibly obtain, the truth about a question that they’re

interested in. They are inquiring into their respective matters, or are about to

engage in such a process of inquiry. Further, they all reasonably ask themselves

how best to pursue their inquiries. They know that their inquiries can go well

or badly, better or worse, depending on what choices they make as to which

sources of evidence to consult: they know that they can make good or bad,

better or worse, choices of evidence-gathering. Cases of this kind will be the

focus of this thesis. To abstract away from the speciﬁcs of the three cases above,

I will be focusing on a rather idealized and simpliﬁed situation, which I call

The Setup. An agent is interested in settling a question, 푄, which I

will call the agent’s research question. The agent can perform one of

a set of mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive acts of evidence-

gathering: acts such that performing them results in the acquisition

of certain pieces of evidence.

How should the agent choose? Under what conditions should we say that

the agent chose the right act of evidence-gathering? Under what conditions

should we say that the agent’s inquiry went well? This thesis is concerned with

the evaluative and normative dimensions intrinsic to the practice of evidence-

gathering: with what makes certain inquiries go well and others badly, with

what makes it the case that one ought to perform certain acts of evidence

collection and not others.1 Here’s an initial answer to these questions, given for

the purposes of circumscribing some more the boundaries of the topic of this

thesis: an inquiry going well, and an agent choosing the right act, is to do with

how informative, conclusive, telling, instructive, revealing, illuminating, the

evidence that the agent collects is with respect to the agent’s research question.

This answer is non-committal and incomplete. First, it doesn’t say what it is

for some evidence to be informative, conclusive, telling, etc. Part of the thesis

will be concerned with ﬁlling in these details. Secondly, it doesn’t specify what

the exact relationship is between the evaluative and normative judgements to

be made about a given case and the evidence collected being informative,

conclusive, telling, etc., in that case. Part of the thesis will again be concerned

with ﬁlling in these details.

The evaluative and normative dimensions that I will be interested in are

intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering in the sense that they hold inde-

pendently of whatever other evaluative and normative considerations may be

at play in each given case of inquiry. An agent may have, for example, moral or

prudential reasons not to consult a certain source of evidence. In these ways, we

can talk about inquiries going well or badly from a moral or prudential point

Let me now zoom out for a moment and consider how the project that I will

pursue in this thesis ﬁts into epistemology as a whole. Any comprehensive

epistemological theory should account for two central aspects of epistemic ac-

tivity. One is belief formation. This aspect has been at the centre-stage of much

of post-Gettier epistemological theorizing. The key questions to ask at this

juncture are: given that a certain agent possesses such-and-such evidence, what

doxastic attitudes should she form? What makes it the case that she should

form precisely those doxastic attitudes in response to that evidence? What

justiﬁes belief? These are among the most fundamental questions in episte-

mology. But an overly narrow focus on them risks suggesting an incomplete

picture of epistemic activity. For it shadows the fact that agents have a degree

of control over what evidence they receive. We get much of our evidence via

perception, simply by navigating our environment and without any conscious

eﬀort directed at collecting it. But sometimes we also decide to look for evidence

bearing on a certain matter, in order to become better informed about it. Nor

is this a feature peculiar to adult human beings: children and non-human an-

imals also actively look for information, such as when a dog uses its olfactory

capacities to individuate the location of a certain object of interest. Following

Jane Friedman, we can call the former kind of evidence acquisition “accidental

learning”, and the latter kind “learning by design”.3 Thus, besides belief for-

mation, epistemic activity involves a second central aspect, evidence collection.

While belief formation concerns doing the best one can given the limited per-

spective on the world that one occupies, evidence collection concerns gaining

a better perspective on the world in the ﬁrst place.

## Chapter 2

## Evidence-Gathering:

## Accuracy and Competence

In this Chapter, I lay out my account of the evaluative and normative dimensions

intrinsic to the practice of evidence-gathering. I will state the conditions under

which an act of evidence-gathering counts as successful, rational, and skillful,

and will further explore the connections between these three aspects. It takes

little reﬂection to notice that evaluating people’s evidence-gathering choices

is not something conﬁned to the epistemology classroom, but is rather one of

the ways in which we ordinarily hold each other accountable qua intelligent

beings. Here are some examples. We would think irrational a philosopher

who tried to ﬁgure out whether body and mind are distinct by reading only

Descartes’ remarks on the matter. We would deem unsuccessful someone who

wanted to gain information about whether there is water on Mars and found

herself no wiser than before, after hours of careful research. And we would

consider incompetent a detective who repeatedly failed to get any closer to the

truth about the crimes they investigate. What follows in this Chapter is an

### 2.1 Initial Remarks

It will be useful to start with some general observations about what kind of

practice evidence-gathering is. First, evidence-gathering is an activity with

an aim, or goal. This plausibly makes evidence-gathering an example of what

Ernest Sosa calls critical domains of value: sets of interrelated entities, activ-

ities, or practices evaluated with respect to a central value, which is valuable

for its own sake relative to that domain.1 Consider as an illustration chess. A

player’s choices can be evaluated vis-à-vis the aim of chess, i.e. checkmating

the opponent. We can say that the player did well or badly, that they should

or shouldn’t have moved a given piece. These evaluative and normative con-

siderations are insulated from moral, prudential or aesthetic evaluations, and

are made possible by the fact that chess is an activity with an aim, or goal.

I will state the aim or goal of evidence-gathering neutrally as improving one’s

epistemic position with respect to one’s question of interest, for example the question

whether 푝. There is a conspicuous literature on what the aim or goal of inquiry

is, which I will turn to consider closely in Chapter 4: knowledge, true belief and

justiﬁed belief are the main contenders.2 In that literature, the aim of inquiry

is often stated in neutral terms as settling a certain question, or as having the

answer to that question, for example the question whether 푝.3 However, this

formulation is too narrow for our purposes. There are cases in which there is

no way for agents to settle whether 푝, but there are ways for them to gain more

information on whether 푝; in such cases, agents may rationally carry out an act

Third, an act of evidence-gathering is an act in the thick sense of the term,

in that it involves choice on the agent’s part. In this respect, we should expect

epistemic evaluations and norms of evidence-gathering to inherit some of the

features of prudential and moral evaluations and norms, which equally concern

choices. And on the other hand, we should expect epistemic evaluations and

norms of evidence-gathering to be unlike epistemic evaluations and norms

governing belief formation, a process which is plausibly not controlled by

choice.

Putting the points so far together, I am ready to state the account that I

turn to develop in detail in the rest of this Chapter. I propose that an act

of evidence-gathering can be evaluated epistemically across three diﬀerent di-

mensions, depending on whether it’s successful, rational, and skillful. Two

notions are deployed to account for these evaluative dimensions: accuracy—in

particular, accuracy gain—and competence. The act is successful to the extent

that it maximises accuracy gain; it is rational to the extent that it maximises

expected accuracy gain; it is skillful to the extent that it manifests the agent’s

competence at collecting accuracy-maximising evidence. In turn, these three

evaluative dimensions combine in diﬀerent ways, the best case being one where

the act of evidence-gathering is skillfully successful: it maximises accuracy gain

and expected accuracy gain with respect to the question of interest to the agent

thanks to the agent’s competence at collecting accuracy-maximising evidence.

### 3.7 Conclusion

What is the correct measure of the usefulness of acquiring certain information,

or of asking certain questions in order to acquire certain information, relative to

the aim of settling a given research question? The accuracy gain model stands

out as the best candidate theory of information value: it is simpler, it ﬁts more

intuitions, and it has greater explanatory power than any of the other available

theories. Information value is to be accounted for in terms of accuracy gain.

This provides a strong case for the accuracy-based component of the account

of Chapter 2. It’s clear that agents are successful to the extent that their evidence-

gathering maximises information value, relative to their research question. And

it’s clear that they are rational to the extent that their evidence-gathering max-

imises expected information value, again relative to their research question.

### 4.1 Two Desiderata

The evidential accuracy account satisﬁes two central desiderata for a satisfatory

According to the credal accuracy theory, the aim of inquiry is to increase the ac-

curacy of one’s credence in the true answer to one’s research question.2 Inquiry

goes well to the extent that the agent’s posterior credence in the true answer

to the research question is accurate. This theory clearly meets the gradabil-

ity desideratum, for there are very many extents to which the agent’s relevant

posterior credence can be accurate.

However, it’s not clear that any interesting notion of information value can

be derived from such a theory. For notice that on this view, any piece of evidence

can be anything from extremely useful to extremely harmful depending on what

the agent makes of it—irrespectively of the agent’s prior credence distribution.

If the agent acquires a piece of misleading evidence and updates on it rationally,

such a piece of evidence will count as of negative value according to the credal

accuracy theory. But the credal accuracy theory will also judge the very same

piece of evidence as of positive value if the very same agent with the very same

prior credences irrationally misinterprets the evidential support relation and

goes on to form a very accurate credence in the true answer to the research

question as a result of acquiring that evidence. One can of course make the

value of information so dependent on facts about the agent’s belief formation,

but this deprives such a notion of much epistemological interest.

### 4.6 Conclusion

This concludes my defence of the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry. The

theory fares better than its three main contenders with respect to the gradability

and information value desiderata. Moreover, it has the resources to meet some

of the most salient objections. No doubt more could be said on both fronts,

either to defend or attack the evidential accuracy theory. At least for now,

however, the theory emerges as the best one on oﬀer. In the next concluding

Chapter, I will look at potential applications and extensions of the theory after

brieﬂy summarizing what has been accomplished so far.

## Conclusions

In this thesis, I have proposed and defended an account of the epistemic ax-

iology and normativity surrounding the practice of evidence-gathering. Let

me brieﬂy summarise each of the account’s building blocks. In the Introduc-

tion, I outlined The Setup, intended to delineate our object of epistemological

study: an agent is interested in settling a question, 푄, and can perform one of

a set of mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive acts of evidence-gathering. I

next presented, in Chapter 2, the accuracy-based virtue-theoretic account, which

speciﬁed the conditions under which such an act of evidence-gathering counts

as successful, rational, and skillful. At the core of the account is the notion

of accuracy gain, which corresponds to the change (positive, negative, or null)

in the accuracy of the agent’s evidential probability in 푄’s true answer that

updating on the evidence collected by performing the chosen act brings about.

The greater the accuracy gain, the more successful the act will be. The greater

the expected accuracy gain, the more rational the act will be. To the extent

that the agent’s act manifests a competence at collecting accuracy-maximising

evidence, it will additionally count as skillful. Finally, if success and rationality

99


<!-- Page 101 -->


are achieved thanks to the agent’s competence, the act will count as skillfully

successful. Chapters 3 and 4 focused on defending the epistemological core

of the accuracy-based virtue-theoretic account, which I called the evidential ac-

curacy theory of inquiry. Chapter 3 argued that accuracy gain independently

provides the best available account of information value. This result provides

strong support in favour of the evidential accuracy theory, for it connects the

success and rationality of an act of evidence-gathering with the usefulness of

the information that the agent obtains by performing it. Chapter 4 looked at

how the evidential accuracy theory fares vis-à-vis three main contenders, argu-

ing that it better ﬁts in with the two desiderata of gradability and information

value and that it can meet three core objections. This concluded my defence of

the evidential accuracy theory of inquiry.

However, it should be clear that my defence of such a theory is only to be

seen as the starting point for epistemological work on the topic of evidence-

gathering. For far from putting to rest philosophical questions about the nature

of inquiry and evidence collection, the account here defended generates yet

more avenues for thought, both by identifying additional problems in the epis-

temology of inquiry itself, and also by connecting the epistemology of inquiry

to other philosophical areas. I now wish to conclude by looking at some of the

avenues for future research suggested by the present account.

First, some research questions arise if one considers the limitations of the

account here defended. One such limitation concerns the narrow focus with

which I’ve been concerned. Recall that our agent in The Setup faces a single

choice between a number of acts of evidence-gathering that she can decide

to perform. However, suppose that we now add an additional element of

complexity to the initial setup: the agent faces a sequence of choices between

diﬀerent acts of evidence-gathering that she can decide to perform. It may be
